questions.q: Your team has argued Redis vs RabbitMQ for 3 weeks and nobody is deciding. As team lead, what do you do first?
questions.hint: Is the argument about the options, or about what to judge them by?

options.text: Ask everyone to go with the most senior person's preference
options.why: When rank decides, the reasoning is lost, and the others don't want to stand behind the result later.

options.text: Agree criteria and weights, build a one-page decision matrix, then name one decision-maker
options.why: The debate moves from preferences to criteria, and one person takes responsibility, with a date.

options.text: Give everyone another week to research
options.why: Without criteria, extra research just becomes new ammunition for the argument. It never reaches a decision.

options.text: Run both and see later
options.why: Running two systems adds cost and complexity. You've only postponed the decision.

questions.q: In a matrix, Doctrine scores 39 and Redis 37. What is the wisest next step?
questions.hint: The gap is only 2 points.

options.text: Doctrine won, end of discussion
options.why: A 2-point gap is within the error of the estimates. Don't be confident about it.

options.text: Re-score so Redis wins
options.why: Bending the result to your preference defeats the whole purpose of a matrix.

options.text: Change the weights to check sensitivity, and discuss which assumption the result hangs on
options.why: When the results are close, the real argument is about weights or assumptions, not the options.

options.text: Drop the matrix and take a vote
options.why: A vote brings preferences back and loses the transparency of the criteria.

questions.q: Which of these decisions deserve more thinking time?
questions.hint: How hard would it be to undo in six months?

options.text: Changing the structure of a public API response
options.why: Mobile apps and partners depend on it. Changing it breaks them, so it is hard to undo.

options.text: Switching the main database engine
options.why: In a system full of data, it is months of work and a big risk.

options.text: Turning on a new button behind a feature flag
options.why: Turning the flag off restores the old state. Undoing takes a minute, so decide quickly.

options.text: Renaming a helper method
options.why: It can be reverted with a single commit today. It isn't expensive.

questions.q: Sarah wants to launch a feature-flag experiment with 60% of the facts. Jake says, "Not until we are 100% sure." Who is right?
questions.hint: Can you walk back through the door?

options.text: Jake, because someone will be blamed if it goes wrong
options.why: For a reversible decision, waiting for 100% certainty loses the opportunity, and a mistake costs little.

options.text: Sarah, because the flag can be switched off to go back. The sign that should trigger a reversal ought to be written down first
options.why: In a small, reversible experiment, learning is the payoff. Written assumptions and triggers cut the risk further.

options.text: Neither. You should stop until more data arrives
options.why: All the facts never arrive. Waiting is also a decision, and it has a price.

questions.q: Your risk register has four risks. Which do you tackle first?
questions.hint: Work out likelihood × impact.

options.text: Complaints about the login page color (likelihood 5, impact 1)
options.why: The likelihood is high but the impact is small, so the score is only 5.

options.text: Only expert on leave (likelihood 4, impact 2)
options.why: The score is 8. It matters, but a cheap action like a runbook is enough.

options.text: Payment gateway down for 2 hours (likelihood 3, impact 5)
options.why: The score is 15, the top of the list. The loss from stopped revenue is enormous.

options.text: Whichever sounds scariest
options.why: Priorities should come from the measured score, not from fear.

questions.q: Two months in, Jake realizes the library he chose doesn't suit the team, though he has written a lot of code with it. What is the best step?
questions.hint: What is already spent won't come back on either path.

options.text: Say nothing and carry on, so the time isn't wasted
options.why: This is the sunk cost trap: spending on the wrong path just keeps growing.

options.text: Admit the mistake himself and weigh what remains: the cost to finish vs the cost to replace
options.why: Speaking first builds trust, and comparing only future costs leads to the right decision.

options.text: Wait for someone else to notice
options.why: The longer you wait, the dearer reversing gets, and a hidden mistake that's found costs you trust.

options.text: Blame the library and tell the team so
options.why: Dodging responsibility destroys trust in your leadership and loses the lesson.

questions.q: You are taking a proposal for a new cloud budget to the CFO. Which opening is best?
questions.hint: What are the CFO's three core questions?

options.text: An explanation of how autoscaling works from CPU load
options.why: That answers an engineer's question. Finance doesn't need it for the decision.

options.text: The approximate monthly cost, the benefit you get, and the loss if you don't do it
options.why: Finance looks for answers to exactly these three questions: how much, what do we get, what if not.

options.text: A feature comparison of the cloud providers
options.why: A comparison may be needed later, but first they need the numbers and consequences for the decision.

options.text: Say "this is modern best practice"
options.why: That is neither a cost nor a gain, so it doesn't help the decision.

questions.q: In the queue design, emails arrive 2 minutes late. How do you tell the product manager?
questions.hint: Product wants to know what is being given up.

options.text: "We're moving to an async model, with eventual consistency."
options.why: Technology words that say nothing about the user experience.

options.text: There is no need to say anything; it is a technical matter
options.why: The late email is visible to users. If product isn't told, a surprise follows.

options.text: "Checkout will finish in 1 second, but the receipt email may arrive up to 2 minutes late."
options.why: It states both the gain and the trade-off in the user's language, so product can decide.

options.text: "Let us know if there are problems with email."
options.why: That doesn't acknowledge the trade-off. It passes the responsibility on.

questions.q: Which of these belong in a good RFC?
questions.hint: What does a reader need in order to decide?

options.text: A description of the problem and the goals
options.why: Without understanding the problem, nobody can judge a proposal.

options.text: At least two options, including "do nothing"
options.why: Showing the options shows the proposal was thought through.

options.text: Risks and the way back
options.why: The decider wants to know how much a mistake would cost and how to undo it.

options.text: The full code of every class
options.why: Code makes the RFC long, and the reader loses the main decision. Code belongs in the PR.

questions.q: Jake's RFC has been hanging for two weeks and nobody is deciding. What went wrong?
questions.hint: Which two things are missing from the top of the RFC when this happens?

options.text: The decider's name and the feedback deadline were never written
options.why: Without these, nobody takes responsibility, and nobody knows when the discussion ends.

options.text: The RFC was too short
options.why: A short RFC is easier to read. Delay comes from unclear ownership.

options.text: More people should have been asked for feedback
options.why: More people means more argument. The real problem is the missing decider.

options.text: There was no diagram
options.why: A diagram helps, but the reason it stalled is the missing structure.

questions.q: In a review, someone said, "How did you even come up with this?" How should they have said it?
questions.hint: Is the question aimed at the person or at the design?

options.text: "That's silly, think again."
options.why: An even harsher personal attack. The author will hide weaknesses.

options.text: Say nothing, and mention it separately after the review
options.why: The whole team needs to know about the risk. Raised in private, the discussion is lost.

options.text: "What does this part do if the payment gateway is slow? Did you look at any alternatives?"
options.why: The question is about one failure path in the design, and it gives room to think of alternatives.

options.text: Stay quiet until the review is over
options.why: If you stay quiet, the risk goes uncaught. The problem is the tone, not the question.

questions.q: You are explaining the new payment design to a regulator's auditor. What helps most?
questions.hint: What proof does an auditor want?

options.text: How fast checkout will be
options.why: That is product's concern. The auditor's question is about following the rules.

options.text: Where card data is kept, and who can view each transaction's audit log, and when
options.why: It is proof of where the data sits and what controls exist, which is what the auditor wants to verify.

options.text: The team size and the sprint plan
options.why: This is not an audit matter. It is internal to the organization.

options.text: The assurance "we are very careful"
options.why: An assurance is not proof. An auditor wants to see records.

questions.q: Sarah wants to change the team's whole query layer, but she holds no manager title. Which approach works best?
questions.hint: Big permission, or small proof?

options.text: Post a long message in Slack telling everyone this is urgent
options.why: An opinion is easy to write and easy to ignore. There is no evidence and no ally.

options.text: Show the problem with numbers, run a pilot in one small module, and win over one respected colleague first
options.why: Evidence, low risk and an ally are all effective ingredients of influence without a title.

options.text: Change the whole system alone and open a PR
options.why: With nobody on board, the PR is large and risky, and there'll be no reviews or support.

options.text: Get the manager to give the order
options.why: An order gets the work done, but not real buy-in, and cooperation will suffer later.

questions.q: Junior developer Jake says, "My query is slow." There is time, and it isn't urgent. What does the senior do?
questions.hint: What do you want him to learn?

options.text: Tell him straight which index to add
options.why: Today's problem gets solved, but Jake doesn't learn to think.

options.text: Fix the code for him
options.why: He learns even less, and he'll depend on you again.

options.text: Ask, "What do you see in EXPLAIN? Which step takes the most time?" and let him think
options.why: Questions teach him to find the cause himself, so next time he can do it alone.

options.text: Say, "It's your job, work it out yourself."
options.why: Leaving someone with no help is not mentoring. He'll just stay stuck.

questions.q: Which of these are signs of good mentoring?
questions.hint: Is the goal the junior's ability to think independently?

options.text: Regular 1:1s where the junior says where they're stuck
options.why: Regularity builds trust, and open conversation catches problems early.

options.text: Sharing stories of your own mistakes
options.why: The junior sees that mistakes are normal, so they don't hide their own.

options.text: Giving a complete answer to every question straight away
options.why: It builds dependence and cuts learning. Outside an emergency, questions are better.

options.text: Fixing every one of the junior's PRs yourself
options.why: They won't learn from any mistake, and your own time gets tied up.

questions.q: Everyone in the meeting was quiet, and the chair said, "So everyone agrees." Later, two people raised serious objections. What went wrong?
questions.hint: What does silence mean?

options.text: Silence was taken as agreement; each person should have been asked by name
options.why: Many people don't voice objections in front of seniors. Asking separately brings them out.

options.text: The meeting was too short
options.why: Even with more time, the quiet people wouldn't have spoken. The gap is elsewhere in the process.

options.text: The proposal was wrong
options.why: The proposal may be fine. The problem was that there was no way to voice an objection.

options.text: More people should have been invited
options.why: The more people in the room, the more likely they are to stay quiet.

questions.q: The team has argued for two weeks, and both options are about equally good. What should Ryan do?
questions.hint: Does the cost of arguing exceed the difference between the options?

options.text: Let the argument run another week
options.why: When the options are equal, more argument just wastes time.

options.text: Set a time limit, name a decider, record dissent and decide
options.why: For a reversible decision between near-equal options, deciding quickly is worth more.

options.text: Take a vote and follow the majority
options.why: A vote makes winning the point and not the reasoning the focus, and nobody owns the decision.

options.text: Drop the subject
options.why: Not deciding is also a decision, and it has a price.

questions.q: After the decision, Sarah notices that new facts show the basis of the decision was wrong. What should she do?
questions.hint: Does disagree and commit apply to new facts too?

options.text: Stay quiet, because the decision is made
options.why: When new facts arrive, you can go back. Staying silent lets the mistake grow.

options.text: Take the new facts to the decider and ask for a rethink
options.why: Commit doesn't mean blind obedience. When the basis changes, the decision can be reconsidered.

options.text: Quietly do it her own way
options.why: Secretly ignoring the decision destroys the team's trust.

options.text: Rally the whole team to her side and rebel
options.why: That is factionalism, not discussion. The right path is to bring the new facts to the decider.

questions.q: The decider says full card numbers will be logged to make debugging easier. Sarah believes this breaks security rules. What does "disagree and commit" say?
questions.hint: Can this decision be undone, and is it only a matter of taste?

options.text: The decision is made; Sarah records her dissent and commits
options.why: A serious security or legal risk is not a dissent to file away. Once the numbers leak, nothing can be undone.

options.text: Sarah raises it as a security objection with the decider and the security or legal team, and the decision waits
options.why: The method is for reversible choices between reasonable options. A serious safety, security or legal objection stops the decision first.

options.text: Sarah quietly builds it her own way without logging the numbers
options.why: Secretly ignoring a decision destroys trust, and the real objection is never answered.

options.text: Take a vote
options.why: A security risk is not settled by votes; it needs an expert's assessment.

questions.q: Marketing says, "We want the offer two weeks before Black Friday." Jake's team wants two months to perfect the whole system. What is the best first step?
questions.hint: What is the offer's real value to the business?

options.text: Tell them it will simply take two months
options.why: It ignores the business deadline; miss the season and the offer has no value.

options.text: Ask marketing which parts are essential before Black Friday, then ship the core in two weeks
options.why: Understanding the goal, you ship the minimum useful part first and polish the rest afterwards.

options.text: Try to do everything in two weeks without asking questions
options.why: Cutting corners on money or security as well causes big losses.

options.text: Ask them to cancel the offer
options.why: It wastes a business opportunity; finding alternatives is the engineer's job.

questions.q: The business says, "The site must be fast." What do you do before designing?
questions.hint: How fast is "fast"?

options.text: Add an index to every query
options.why: Adding indexes without knowing what is slow, or how slow, is wasted work and slows writes.

options.text: Ask for numbers: which page, under how many seconds, for how many users
options.why: You can't measure "fast" without numbers. Once the target is set, you can decide which design is enough.

options.text: Move the whole app to a new framework
options.why: A huge decision without knowing the problem, with high risk and cost.

options.text: Buy a more powerful server
options.why: Spending without knowing the cause; if the problem is in the code or a query, a server won't fix it.

questions.q: Two projects: X costs $40,000 and earns $80,000 a year; Y costs $60,000 and earns $30,000 a year. What is X's payback?
questions.hint: Monthly gain = $80,000 ÷ 12.

options.text: 6 months
options.why: Monthly gain is about $6,700; $40,000 ÷ $6,700 ≈ 6 months. (X earns $80,000 a year, twice its cost.)

options.text: 12 months
options.why: If a year's gain is twice the cost, the cost is earned back in half a year.

options.text: 24 months
options.why: This is closer to Y. X's gain is much higher.

options.text: It can't be said
options.why: With the cost and the monthly gain, payback is easy to calculate.

questions.q: Which of these can be cut when time is short?
questions.hint: A mistake is cheap and easy to fix.

options.text: Styling of the admin pages
options.why: Customers don't see them, and they are easy to fix later.

options.text: Speed of a rarely used report
options.why: It slows down a few people's work, so the harm is small, and it can be fixed later.

options.text: Payment tests
options.why: A money mistake is hard to fix, and trust is lost too.

options.text: The rules for storing users' passwords
options.why: There is no room to give on security; once leaked, it can't be undone.

questions.q: A new project will store users' personal data. When should you look at the legal rules?
questions.hint: How hard is it to move data to a different location?

options.text: The week before launch
options.why: By then the database and region are fixed, and changing them takes months.

options.text: At the start of design, with a data list and the five questions
options.why: If location, retention and access are settled at the start, the design is right the first time.

options.text: When the auditor arrives
options.why: By then the problem is deep, and building proof is hard.

options.text: Never; the law is not an engineer's concern
options.why: Engineers own the design; they have to take the constraints on board together with a legal expert.

questions.q: A rule says rejected applicants' ID photos must be deleted after 90 days. What do you build?
questions.hint: A rule you can't prove you followed is only half followed.

options.text: A note in the team wiki asking admins to delete old photos when they remember
options.why: Manual steps get forgotten, and nothing proves they happened.

options.text: Hide the photos in the admin screen but keep them in the database
options.why: Hidden is not deleted. The data still exists, so the rule is broken, and a leak would still expose it.

options.text: A nightly job that deletes the photos and writes an audit_log row for each one
options.why: The rule is enforced automatically, and the audit rows are the proof for the auditor.

options.text: Nothing yet; wait until the auditor asks
options.why: By then photos older than 90 days exist, and you can't show a history of following the rule.

questions.q: You took on debt to launch quickly. What is the best next step?
questions.hint: The interest on hidden debt keeps growing.

options.text: Write the debt down, set a sprint to repay it, and tell the business about the risk
options.why: Visible debt stays under control: everyone knows, and there is a repayment plan.

options.text: Tell nobody and hope nothing happens
options.why: A hidden debt shows up as a sudden big problem.

options.text: Get busy with the next feature
options.why: If a debt isn't written down, nobody remembers it, and it never gets repaid.

options.text: Stop all work and repay the debt first
options.why: Repaying matters, but the timing has to be set against the business's priorities.

questions.q: Our feature depends on the payment team's API, which is still in design. We need it in 2 weeks. What do you do?
questions.hint: What happens when the delay is only found at the last minute?

options.text: Wait; they will surely deliver on time
options.why: Hoping is not a plan. The delay will surface when there is no time left to act.

options.text: Flag it red in the dependency register, talk to the owner directly, and line up a fallback or a stub if needed
options.why: Knowing the risk early leaves time for a fix, and talking directly to the owner works best.

options.text: Write the payment team's code yourself
options.why: Stepping across another team's boundary breeds conflict and mistakes.

options.text: Drop the feature from the roadmap
options.why: It hurts the business. Look for a solution first.

questions.q: One team handles checkout, a complex pricing ML model and CI/CD, and everything is slow. What do you do?
questions.hint: Where is the cognitive load highest?

options.text: Add five more people to the team
options.why: A bigger team adds coordination cost. The core problem is load, not headcount.

options.text: Move CI/CD to a platform team and the model to a complicated-subsystem team; checkout stays with its own flow
options.why: Separating the hard and tooling work lowers the stream team's load.

options.text: Train everyone in everything
options.why: The load doesn't drop; trying to learn everything, nobody goes deep on anything.

options.text: Change nothing and tell them to "work harder"
options.why: A structural problem isn't fixed by effort.

questions.q: A start-up with 6 engineers is told to form a stream-aligned, a platform, an enabling and a complicated-subsystem team. What is the best response?
questions.hint: Does the pain the types cure exist yet?

options.text: Do it; four teams of one or two people each
options.why: Each tiny team still needs the same skills, and the hand-offs between them cost more than they save.

options.text: Keep one team for now, and split when work queues behind one person or nobody understands the whole system
options.why: The types cure overload. With 6 people one team can hold the whole system, so splitting only adds hand-offs.

options.text: Hire 20 more engineers so there are enough people for four teams
options.why: Hiring to fit a diagram reverses the logic. Structure follows the load, not the other way around.

options.text: Ignore team design forever
options.why: Revisit it as the team grows. The caveat is about timing, not about never splitting.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a good estimate?
questions.hint: Why is a single number dangerous?

options.text: A range (say, 15 to 21 days)
options.why: A range shows the uncertainty and avoids a false promise.

options.text: The assumptions the estimate depends on
options.why: If the assumptions are wrong, you can see why it ran late.

options.text: Identifying the biggest source of uncertainty
options.why: Shrink that first and the whole estimate becomes more reliable.

options.text: A fixed number that the manager prefers
options.why: Changing the number to suit the manager doesn't shrink the work; the delay just shows up later.

questions.q: Three tasks have (best, likely, worst) of 2, 4 and 10. What is the expected time?
questions.hint: (best + 4 × likely + worst) ÷ 6.

options.text: 4.7 days
5.3 days
options.why: That is the simple average of the three numbers (16 ÷ 3); PERT weights the likely value more.

options.text: 10 days
options.why: That is only the worst case; the worst doesn't always happen.

options.text: 2 days
options.why: That is only the best case, an optimistic guess.

questions.q: Two tasks have a spread of 3 days and 4 days. What is the spread of the two together?
questions.hint: Spreads are squared, added, then rooted.

options.text: 7 days
options.why: Adding spreads assumes both tasks go badly at the same time. They rarely do, so you add the squares and take the root.

options.text: 5 days
3.5 days
options.why: That is the average. Two tasks together are less certain than their average, not equally so.

options.text: 12 days
options.why: Multiplying has no meaning here; spreads combine through their squares.

questions.q: A new vendor's salesperson says, "You will always get your data back, don't worry." What do you do?
questions.hint: Which is binding: a spoken word or the contract?

options.text: Sign, trusting them; the vendor seems good
options.why: A spoken promise is not proof. Once the relationship sours, nobody will honor it.

options.text: Get the data-return format and timing written into the contract, and have legal check the terms
options.why: If it isn't in the contract, it isn't binding; only written terms protect you.

options.text: Skip the vendor and build everything ourselves
options.why: Build vs buy is a separate decision. The problem here is getting the terms clear.

options.text: Sign because of the low price
options.why: Deciding on price without knowing the price-rise terms and exit costs is dangerous.

questions.q: After the interview, everyone liked candidate A, but on the scorecard candidate B scored higher. What do you do?
questions.hint: Which is more reliable: a liking, or evidence?

options.text: Hire A, because everybody liked them
options.why: A liking can be full of bias; evidence should come first.

options.text: Look at the evidence column, discuss why liking and scores differ, and run another round if needed
options.why: Finding where they differ exposes bias, and the decision rests on evidence.

options.text: Throw out the scorecard and take a vote
options.why: In a vote, liking wins again.

options.text: Hire neither
options.why: With evidence, there is a case for hiring B. Rejecting both is an overreaction.

questions.q: The team has 2,000 users and 5 developers. Everyone says, "Let's move to microservices." What do you ask?
questions.hint: Where is the problem?

options.text: "For which problem? Show it in numbers, and what do the alternatives cost?"
options.why: Measuring the problem shows whether the extra complexity is justified; for a team of 5, it often isn't.

options.text: "The big companies do it, so we do too."
options.why: Their problems (millions of users, hundreds of engineers) aren't ours.

options.text: "I don't know if it'll be good, let's just try it, for six months."
options.why: A big investment without measuring the problem; start with a small spike instead.

options.text: "No, microservices are always bad."
options.why: They aren't always bad; they work for bigger teams or different scale. The answer depends on the problem.

questions.q: In evaluating a new database, which proof is the most credible?
questions.hint: Who has a stake?

options.text: The vendor's conference talk
options.why: The vendor has a sales interest and won't talk about weaknesses.

options.text: A write-up of two years in production from a company of our size, with its limitations
options.why: They know the problems that only show up in real use, and the size matches.

options.text: How many stars it has on GitHub
options.why: Popularity doesn't mean it solves our problem.

options.text: The announcement of the newest version
options.why: The newer it is, the more unknown problems it has.

questions.q: You have 2 hours a week to learn. Which of these are good investments?
questions.hint: What will still be useful in 10 years?

options.text: Reading about transactions and isolation levels and writing it up in your own words
options.why: Fundamental ideas help in any tool.

options.text: Getting stuck on a problem at work and running a small spike on it
options.why: Learning by doing, tied to real work, lasts.

options.text: Building a "hello world" in a new framework every week
options.why: You don't get depth, and most of it is never used.

options.text: Scrolling tech trends on social media without doing anything
options.why: Watching passively isn't learning; it feeds the hype and not your understanding.

questions.q: For a small admin page, Sarah wants an interface and a repository for every class; Jake says use Doctrine directly. What do you say?
questions.hint: Is there any chance of change?

options.text: Sarah is right; rules must always be followed
options.why: The rule's purpose is absent here; the extra layer only adds complexity.

options.text: Jake's simple path works if the data source is unlikely to change. Write down the reason for the decision.
options.why: With no purpose, the simple path is better; a written reason helps later if it needs to change.

options.text: Whoever is older gets their way
options.why: Age or rank is not an argument.

options.text: Even for money work, take the simple path
options.why: Simplifying around money and security is risky; that needs separate thought.

questions.q: Which of these are part of owning a decision?
questions.hint: What do you do after making the decision?

options.text: Fixing in advance which numbers will tell you the decision is right
options.why: With the measures fixed first, you can't pick numbers you like afterwards.

options.text: Putting a six-month review in the calendar
options.why: Forgetting is natural; fixing the date in advance makes sure you look back.

options.text: Speaking up yourself first when a mistake is spotted
options.why: Saying it first cuts the damage and builds trust.

options.text: Forgetting the matter after the decision and moving on to other work
options.why: Responsibility doesn't end there; the results arrive over time.

questions.q: At the six-month review, message volume turns out to be ten times what was expected. What is Ryan's best response?
questions.hint: What do you do when an assumption was wrong?

options.text: Bury the number, since the decision was Ryan's
options.why: Hiding it makes the problem grow, and it comes back later as a major incident.

options.text: Say the assumption was wrong, and start a rethink with a new decision and a plan to repay the debt
options.why: Honestly admitting the mistake and correcting it quickly is what owning a decision means.

options.text: Ask the business to cut the messages
options.why: Treating real business growth as the problem points the wrong way.

options.text: What was known at the time was enough, and nothing needs to change
options.why: When new facts arrive, changing the decision is the smart thing to do.

questions.q: Jake's filled-in evaluation shows 5 requests a second at peak, the server at 15% CPU, and 6 months of cost. What do you write?
questions.hint: Does the evidence show a problem that the solution fixes?

options.text: Decision: No, because no measured problem. Revisit if peak passes a stated number.
options.why: The numbers show no scale problem. A written trigger lets the answer change when the facts change.

options.text: Decision: Yes, we will need it when we grow.
options.why: This is the "might need it later" reasoning. Build for today's measured problem and revisit with a trigger.

options.text: Decision: Yes, because the big companies use it.
options.why: Their problems (hundreds of engineers) are not in the evidence.

options.text: Decision: No. Say nothing more, so it is not argued again.
options.why: Without the reason and the trigger, the debate returns every few months with no facts to settle it.
